questions.q: Which strike did Theodore Roosevelt help end in 1902 by convening mine owners and union leaders and backing arbitration?
questions.explain: Roosevelt threatened federal action, and an arbitration commission he appointed ended the strike with a raise for the miners.

questions.q: The Budget and Accounting Act of 1921 required the president to do what each year?
options: Veto any spending bill above a fixed cap
Submit an annual budget for the whole government
Report gold reserves to the Senate
questions.explain: The act created the Bureau of the Budget, now the OMB, so the president rather than separate agencies presented the government's budget.

questions.q: The Executive Office of the President, which houses the White House staff, was created in 1939 following recommendations of which body?
questions.explain: The Brownlow Committee urged more presidential staff, and Franklin Roosevelt created the Executive Office of the President in 1939.

questions.q: Which 1947 law created the National Security Council to advise the president on foreign and defense policy?
questions.explain: The National Security Act of 1947 also created the Central Intelligence Agency and a unified National Military Establishment.

questions.q: Which law created the Council of Economic Advisers to counsel the president on economic policy?
questions.explain: The Employment Act of 1946 committed the federal government to promoting maximum employment and created the Council of Economic Advisers.

questions.q: To enforce a court-ordered desegregation of Little Rock Central High School in 1957, President Eisenhower sent which force?
questions.explain: Eisenhower federalized the Arkansas National Guard and sent paratroopers of the 101st Airborne to escort nine Black students into the school.

questions.q: During the October 1962 Cuban missile crisis, what was the group of senior advisers Kennedy convened called?
options: The Executive Committee of the National Security Council
questions.explain: Known as ExComm, the group helped Kennedy weigh air strikes against a naval blockade, which he called a quarantine.

questions.q: Under the War Powers Resolution of 1973, within how many hours must the president report to Congress after sending forces into hostilities?
questions.explain: Congress passed the resolution over President Nixon's veto, requiring a report within 48 hours and limiting deployments to 60 days without authorization.

questions.q: Which two leaders signed the 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty at the White House?
options: Gamal Abdel Nasser and David Ben-Gurion
questions.explain: President Carter hosted Sadat and Begin; the treaty followed the 1978 Camp David Accords.

questions.q: Which two leaders shook hands at the White House in 1993 after signing the Israeli-Palestinian Declaration of Principles?
questions.explain: President Clinton stood between Rabin and Arafat at the September 1993 signing of the first Oslo agreement.

questions.q: What was the name of the missile-defense research program Reagan proposed in a March 1983 televised address?
questions.explain: Critics nicknamed the Strategic Defense Initiative 'Star Wars'; it sought defenses against ballistic missiles.

questions.q: What share of a state's 1860 voters had to swear loyalty under Lincoln's 1863 plan before the state could form a new government?
questions.explain: Lincoln's Proclamation of Amnesty and Reconstruction, the Ten Percent Plan, was criticized by Radical Republicans as too lenient.

questions.q: Andrew Johnson's 1868 impeachment grew out of his attempt to remove which cabinet officer?
options: Secretary of the Navy Gideon Welles
questions.explain: Johnson's removal of Stanton violated the Tenure of Office Act; the Senate fell one vote short of conviction.

questions.q: What nickname was given to Andrew Jackson's informal advisers who met with him outside formal cabinet sessions?
questions.explain: Critics said Jackson relied on friends and newspaper allies more than on his formal cabinet.

questions.q: What did the 25th Amendment, ratified in 1967, establish?
options: A ban on poll taxes and literacy tests in federal and state elections
The vote for citizens aged eighteen
Rules for presidential disability and vice presidential vacancies
questions.explain: It was ratified after the Kennedy assassination had highlighted gaps in the rules of succession and disability.

questions.q: What was the subject of Franklin Roosevelt's first fireside chat in March 1933?
options: The banking crisis and reopening of banks
The plan to enlarge the Supreme Court
Aid to Britain before Pearl Harbor
questions.explain: Roosevelt used radio to explain in plain language how the bank holiday and reopening of sound banks would work.

questions.q: In July 1932 President Hoover ordered the army, led by Douglas MacArthur, to clear which group from Washington?
options: The Bonus Army of World War I veterans
questions.explain: The veterans had demanded early payment of their service certificates, and the clearing damaged Hoover's reputation.

questions.q: On what charges did the House of Representatives impeach President Clinton in December 1998?
options: Abuse of power and contempt of Congress
questions.explain: The Senate acquitted Clinton in February 1999 on both articles.

questions.q: Which new agency was created by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act that Obama signed?
questions.explain: Dodd-Frank responded to the 2008 financial crisis with new rules for banks and a consumer protection agency.

questions.q: The tie between Jefferson and Burr in the 1800 Electoral College led to ratification of which amendment?
questions.explain: The Twelfth Amendment, ratified in 1804, had electors vote separately for president and vice president.

questions.q: Which president is the only one to have been married in the White House?
questions.explain: Grover Cleveland married Frances Folsom in the White House's Blue Room on June 2, 1886. He is the only president to wed in the White House.

questions.q: Truman's Executive Order 9835 of 1947 created what?
options: A ban on Communist Party membership
A loyalty program for federal employees
questions.explain: It authorized loyalty review boards to examine federal workers, a landmark of early Cold War domestic anticommunism.

questions.q: Who was named the first director of the Peace Corps in 1961?
questions.explain: Kennedy created the Peace Corps by executive order in March 1961, and Congress authorized it that fall.

questions.q: Which agency did President Nixon establish in 1970 to consolidate federal pollution control programs?
options: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration
questions.explain: Nixon sent a reorganization plan to Congress, and the EPA began operating in December 1970.

questions.q: In the 1972 Shanghai Communique after Nixon's visit to China, the United States acknowledged what position?
options: That Taiwan should become an independent state under US protection
That Chinese on both sides of the Strait maintain there is one China
That US forces would leave Japan
questions.explain: The word acknowledged was ambiguous, but the communique opened the way to normalized relations in 1979.

questions.q: Which painting in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda shows the Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto reaching a great river in 1541?
questions.explain: William Powell's painting shows de Soto's expedition at the Mississippi; it is one of eight historical paintings in the Rotunda.

questions.q: The Capitol Rotunda painting Embarkation of the Pilgrims depicts the Pilgrims leaving which Dutch port in 1620?
questions.explain: Robert Weir's painting shows the Pilgrims leaving Delfshaven; they later sailed from England on the Mayflower.

questions.q: Which Virginia colonist's baptism is shown in a large painting in the Capitol Rotunda?
questions.explain: John Chapman's painting depicts Pocahontas's baptism as a Christian, a Jamestown-era event.

questions.q: The U.S. Capitol Rotunda painting by John Trumbull showing George Washington resigning his commission in 1783 is set in which city?
questions.explain: Congress met in Annapolis, Maryland, when Washington returned his military authority to civilian control.

questions.q: How many Revolutionary War paintings by John Trumbull hang in the Capitol Rotunda?
questions.explain: They show the Declaration of Independence, the surrenders at Saratoga and Yorktown, and Washington resigning his commission.

questions.q: Which civil rights leader and Georgia congressman lay in state in the Capitol Rotunda in July 2020?
questions.explain: Lewis had been a leader of SNCC and spoke at the 1963 March on Washington.

questions.q: Under a law of 1864, how many statues may each state contribute to the National Statuary Hall Collection?
questions.explain: The 1864 law created the collection in the old House chamber; today the statues stand throughout the Capitol, two from each state.

questions.q: Which enslaved worker helped cast the Statue of Freedom for the top of the Capitol dome?
questions.explain: Clark Mills's foundry turned to Philip Reid, one of its enslaved workers, to separate the plaster model into sections for casting in bronze.

questions.q: Which architect designed the cast-iron Capitol dome that was built during the Civil War?
questions.explain: Walter's iron dome rose between 1855 and 1866, so most of it went up during the Civil War.

questions.q: Which three suffrage pioneers are portrayed in the marble Portrait Monument by Adelaide Johnson that stands in the Capitol Rotunda?
options: Sojourner Truth, Harriet Tubman and Susan B. Anthony
Alice Paul, Carrie Chapman Catt and Lucy Stone
Harriet Beecher Stowe, Mott and Lucy Stone
Lucretia Mott, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony
questions.explain: It was unveiled in the Rotunda in 1921, moved to the Crypt soon after, and returned to the Rotunda in 1997.

questions.q: In his Second Inaugural Address, how did Lincoln suggest the Civil War should be understood?
options: As a possible divine judgment on North and South for slavery
As a tragic mistake that skilled diplomacy might have avoided
As a rebellion led by a handful of Southern leaders
As a war that would end with Southern independence
questions.explain: Lincoln said that if God willed the war to continue until slavery's wrongs were paid for, the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous.

questions.q: Whose 1981 inauguration was the first held on the West Front of the Capitol, facing the National Mall?
questions.explain: Most inaugurations from 1829 through 1977 were held on the East Front; Congress's inaugural committee chose the roomier West Front in 1980.

questions.q: Who began the Capitol Rotunda's historical frieze that wraps around the dome's base but died before it was complete?
questions.explain: Brumidi died in 1880, and Filippo Costaggini and later Allyn Cox completed the work.

questions.q: Who laid the cornerstone of the United States Capitol in a ceremony on September 18, 1793?
questions.explain: Washington took part in a Masonic ceremony for the building that Congress first used in 1800.

questions.q: The Senate adopted its first cloture rule in 1917 after a filibuster against which Woodrow Wilson proposal?
questions.explain: Wilson denounced the filibustering senators as a little group of willful men, and the Senate then adopted Rule 22.

questions.q: In 2017 the Senate for the first time allowed a simple majority to end debate on which kind of nomination?
questions.explain: Majority Leader McConnell's change came during the Gorsuch nomination; in 2013 Democrats had done the same for other nominees.

questions.q: Which former White House aide revealed in July 1973 that Nixon had a secret taping system in the Oval Office?
questions.explain: Butterfield's testimony to the Senate Watergate committee led to the fight over the tapes.

questions.q: Which attorney asked Senator Joseph McCarthy, 'Have you no sense of decency?' during the 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings?
questions.explain: Welch represented the Army, and the televised exchange helped turn public opinion against McCarthy.

questions.q: What action did the Senate take against Joseph McCarthy in December 1954?
options: It removed him from all committees permanently
It suspended him for one year
questions.explain: The vote of condemnation, usually called a censure, followed the televised hearings and ended his influence.

questions.q: Which Republican Senate leader helped negotiate the compromise that led to cloture on the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
questions.explain: The Senate voted 71 to 29 for cloture on June 10, 1964, ending the filibuster after Dirksen helped negotiate a substitute bill.

questions.q: Which two senators voted against the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in August 1964?
questions.explain: The Senate approved the resolution 88 to 2; the House vote was unanimous.

questions.q: Which senator gave the 1950 'Declaration of Conscience' speech criticizing McCarthyism?
questions.explain: Smith of Maine delivered it on June 1, 1950, and six other Republican senators signed it; it never named McCarthy directly.

questions.q: In 1805 the Senate tried and acquitted which Supreme Court justice on impeachment charges?
questions.explain: The House had impeached Chase for partisan conduct on the bench, but the Senate did not reach two-thirds on any article.

questions.q: After Henry Clay's omnibus bill failed in 1850, which senator steered the Compromise of 1850 through Congress as separate bills?
questions.explain: Douglas passed the measures one at a time by building different majorities for each.

questions.q: The Senate's rejection of which agreement in 1919 and 1920 kept the US out of the League of Nations?
questions.explain: The Senate defeated the treaty and League covenant by March 1920 after opposition led by Henry Cabot Lodge.

questions.q: Who in 1870 became the first African American to serve in the US Senate?
questions.explain: Revels of Mississippi was seated in 1870 during Reconstruction.

questions.q: Which senator was brutally caned by a South Carolina congressman on the Senate floor in 1856?
questions.explain: Preston Brooks attacked Sumner after his speech The Crime Against Kansas.

questions.q: Who became the first Black woman to serve in the US Senate, taking office in 1993 after her election the year before?
questions.explain: Carol Moseley Braun, a Democrat from Illinois, won her Senate race in 1992 and took office in 1993 as the first Black woman in the Senate.

questions.q: How much did the United States pay Russia for Alaska under the treaty the Senate approved in 1867?
questions.explain: Secretary of State William Seward negotiated the purchase, which critics mocked as Seward's Folly.

questions.q: The Senate Watergate Committee in 1973 was chaired by which senator from North Carolina?
questions.explain: Ervin chaired the committee, with Howard Baker as its senior Republican, and the hearings were broadcast live on television.

questions.q: Strom Thurmond's filibuster of 24 hours and 18 minutes, the longest Senate speech until 2025, targeted which law?
questions.explain: The 1957 act was the first federal civil rights law since Reconstruction.

questions.q: Under the Constitution, how many senators must vote to ratify a treaty?
questions.explain: Article II gives this role to the Senate, which has rejected high-profile treaties like Versailles.

questions.q: The Senate's Rule 22 on cloture requires how many votes to end debate on most legislation?
questions.explain: The Senate lowered the threshold from two-thirds to three-fifths in 1975.

questions.q: In 1890 Speaker Thomas B. Reed ended the 'disappearing quorum' by doing what?
options: Suspending members who refused to answer the roll call
Counting members present even if they refused to vote
Giving the minority leader a veto
questions.explain: Reed's rule let the majority pass bills even when the minority refused to answer roll calls.

questions.q: The 1910 revolt against Speaker Joseph Cannon reduced his power by removing him from which body?
questions.explain: Progressive Republicans and Democrats joined to remove the Speaker from the Rules Committee and enlarge it with members elected by the House. In 1911 the Speaker also lost the power to make committee assignments.

questions.q: In 1847 Representative Abraham Lincoln's 'spot resolutions' challenged which president's account of how the Mexican-American War began?
questions.explain: Lincoln demanded to know the exact spot where Mexican forces had shed American blood on American soil.

questions.q: Under the Twelfth Amendment, when the House chooses a president, how are votes counted?
options: Each state delegation casts one vote
The Speaker decides in a tie
questions.explain: The same one-vote-per-state rule decided the 1800 election under the original Constitution, and in 1825 the House used it under the Twelfth Amendment to choose John Quincy Adams over Andrew Jackson.

questions.q: Who was the first African American to serve in the US House of Representatives, seated in December 1870?
questions.explain: Rainey of South Carolina was elected during Reconstruction and served until 1879.

questions.q: Who served as Speaker of the House for 17 years, the longest of the 20th century?
questions.explain: Rayburn of Texas held the post in three stretches between 1940 and 1961.

questions.q: In 1954, nationalists from which place fired weapons from the House gallery, wounding five representatives?
questions.explain: The attackers sought attention for Puerto Rican independence; all of the wounded representatives survived.

questions.q: Which 1964 Supreme Court case required congressional districts within a state to have roughly equal populations?
questions.explain: The ruling relied on Article I's command that representatives be chosen by the people of the several states.

questions.q: Baker v. Carr (1962) held that what kind of claims were open to federal courts?
questions.explain: The Court ruled that malapportionment claims were not political questions, which opened the door to one person, one vote.

questions.q: The Reapportionment Act of 1929 capped the size of the House of Representatives at how many members?
questions.explain: The act made reapportionment automatic after each census with the House held at 435; it briefly had 437 members after Alaska and Hawaii statehood.

questions.q: In 1994 Republicans won control of the House for the first time since which year?
questions.explain: Republicans ran on Newt Gingrich's Contract with America, and Gingrich became Speaker when the new Congress met.

questions.q: Which president revived the practice of delivering the State of the Union in person to Congress in 1913?
questions.explain: Thomas Jefferson had ended the oral practice, and presidents sent written messages for more than a century.

questions.q: Who became the first woman Speaker of the House in 2007?
questions.explain: Pelosi of California was elected Speaker by Democrats after their 2006 victory.

questions.q: John Quincy Adams, who died in the Capitol in 1848, served in the House after being what?
questions.explain: Adams served in the House from 1831 until his death in the Capitol on February 23, 1848.

questions.q: The House Un-American Activities Committee in 1947 held hearings on Communist influence in which industry?
questions.explain: Ten uncooperative witnesses, known as the Hollywood Ten, were cited for contempt of Congress.

questions.q: Elbridge Gerry's name became attached to a practice after Massachusetts drew an oddly shaped district in 1812. What was the practice?
options: Drawing district lines for partisan advantage
Delaying legislative votes through very long speeches
questions.explain: The salamander-shaped district was dubbed a Gerrymander by critics in a Boston newspaper.

questions.q: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) strengthened federal power by interpreting which clause broadly?
options: The Full Faith and Credit Clause
questions.explain: Chief Justice Marshall held that navigation between states was commerce Congress could regulate, overriding a New York steamboat monopoly.

questions.q: Dartmouth College v. Woodward (1819) held that a state could not alter a college's charter because of which clause?
questions.explain: Marshall treated a corporate charter as a contract, a ruling that protected private institutions and business from state interference.

questions.q: Fletcher v. Peck (1810) was the first Supreme Court decision to strike down which kind of law?
questions.explain: The Court held that Georgia's repeal of a land grant impaired the obligation of contracts.

questions.q: Martin v. Hunter's Lessee (1816) confirmed the Supreme Court's power to do what?
options: Veto acts of Congress before passage
Review state court decisions on federal law
questions.explain: Justice Story held that the Court could review state court rulings that involved federal questions.

questions.q: Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge (1837) favored which principle in Chief Justice Taney's Court?
options: Perpetual protection of all corporate charters from competition
Public interest in new enterprise over implied monopolies
questions.explain: Taney held that charters should be read narrowly so that new competitors could build, encouraging growth.

questions.q: Ex parte Milligan (1866) held that military tribunals could not try civilians when what was true?
options: Civil courts were open and functioning
The president was absent from Washington
questions.explain: The Court said martial law could not be applied where civil courts were able to operate.

questions.q: In Schenck v. United States (1919), Justice Holmes introduced which test for limiting speech?
questions.explain: Holmes wrote that speech creating a clear and present danger of evils Congress may prevent can be punished, in the context of antiwar leaflets.

questions.q: Gitlow v. New York (1925) was an early step in which process?
options: Allowing police wiretaps without any warrant at all
Applying Bill of Rights guarantees to the states
questions.explain: The Court assumed that freedoms of speech and press are protected against state action by the Fourteenth Amendment.

questions.q: Near v. Minnesota (1931) limited which government action?
questions.explain: Chief Justice Hughes wrote that prior restraints on publication were allowed only in exceptional cases.

questions.q: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952) ruled against which president's action?
options: Eisenhower's use of troops at Little Rock
questions.explain: The Court said Truman had no authority to seize the mills during the Korean War without congressional approval.

questions.q: Cooper v. Aaron (1958) declared what about state officials and Supreme Court rulings?
options: They may delay compliance for as long as ten years if needed
They may interpose to nullify rulings
They are exempt if a majority objects
They are bound by the Court's constitutional decisions
questions.explain: The Court rejected the Little Rock school board's request to postpone integration of Central High School, holding that state officials could not defy Brown v. Board of Education.

questions.q: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) required public officials suing for libel to prove what?
questions.explain: The Court held that false statements about public officials are protected unless made with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth.

questions.q: Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964) upheld Title II of the Civil Rights Act under which power?
questions.explain: The Court held that Congress could bar discrimination in public accommodations because it affected interstate commerce.

questions.q: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) allows government to punish advocacy only when it is directed to inciting what?
questions.explain: The decision made the test for punishable advocacy stricter, focusing on imminence.

questions.q: Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971) created a three-part test for cases involving which clause?
questions.explain: The test asked about a secular purpose, primary effect, and entanglement of government with religion.

questions.q: In Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978), the Court ruled that a medical school could not do what?
options: Use fixed racial quotas in admissions
questions.explain: Justice Powell's controlling opinion allowed race as one factor but not a rigid quota.

questions.q: Texas v. Johnson (1989) held that what is protected as symbolic speech?
questions.explain: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Court ruled 5-4 that burning the American flag in protest is symbolic speech protected by the First Amendment, striking down a Texas law.

questions.q: United States v. Lopez (1995) was the first case in decades to limit Congress's use of which power?
questions.explain: The Court struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990.

questions.q: Bush v. Gore (2000) ended the controversy over the presidential vote in which state?
questions.explain: The Court halted the recount, leaving George W. Bush with Florida's electoral votes.

questions.q: Lawrence v. Texas (2003) struck down state laws criminalizing what?
questions.explain: The Court overruled Bowers v. Hardwick on due process grounds.

questions.q: Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held that the government may not ban what?
questions.explain: The decision relied on the First Amendment and super PACs soon followed.

questions.q: Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down which part of the Voting Rights Act?
questions.explain: The Court held the formula outdated, though Congress could write a new one.

questions.q: Who in 2016 became the first woman and first African American to serve as Librarian of Congress?
questions.explain: Hayden, a former head of the Enoch Pratt Free Library in Baltimore, was nominated by President Obama.

questions.q: Which passage in Jefferson's draft of the Declaration of Independence did Congress remove?
options: His charge that the king had forced slavery on the colonies
His detailed list of grievances against the British Parliament
His call for a new government
questions.explain: Jefferson's draft blamed King George III for slavery, and Congress cut the passage, partly to keep South Carolina and Georgia on board.

questions.q: Which folklorist recorded blues musician Muddy Waters in Mississippi in 1941 for the Library of Congress?
questions.explain: Lomax, working for the Library of Congress with Fisk University's John Work, recorded the young Muddy Waters at Stovall, Mississippi.

questions.q: Who headed the Farm Security Administration photography project whose images are held at the Library of Congress?
questions.explain: Stryker directed photographers such as Dorothea Lange and Walker Evans to document rural poverty and the Great Depression.

questions.q: Alexis de Tocqueville and Gustave de Beaumont first traveled to the United States in 1831 to study which institution?
questions.explain: The report on prisons became their official reason for the trip, and Tocqueville later wrote Democracy in America.
